subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Complete the following conversions. i) Benzoic acid to benzamide  ii) Aniline to p-bromoaniline

verification.note: Unit 18 (Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.115-120, from the shaded sub-box "ORGANIC COMPOUNDS CONTAINING NITROGEN" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.116 as VSAQ 8. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECK: both printed routes are correct and are kept — benzoic acid with NH₃ to the ammonium salt then heat, and aniline through acetanilide and p-bromoacetanilide back to p-bromoaniline. BOOK GAP, filled here: the printed answer draws the three-step aniline route but never says WHY the amine is acetylated first. Without acetylation, bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline in one step, because –NH₂ activates the ring so strongly. That reason is the whole point of the route and is added. NOTATION: the book draws benzene rings; this card writes the same compounds as linear text with the reagents in brackets after the arrow.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Benzoic acid to benzamide
lines: Benzoic acid is treated with ammonia and the
ammonium benzoate formed is then heated.
steps.why: An acid and ammonia react as an acid and a base, so the salt ammonium benzoate is what forms in the cold. Heating that salt removes one molecule of water and leaves the amide. The heat is therefore a required condition, not an optional one: it is the step that makes the amide.
common_mistakes: Writing benzoic acid straight to benzamide with NH₃ alone. The salt forms first and must be heated.
Writing the ammonium salt as C₆H₅COONH₂ or C₆H₅CONH₄. Ammonium benzoate is C₆H₅COONH₄, and heating it gives the amide and water.
steps.memory_tip: Without heat the answer stops at ammonium benzoate. The Δ is what turns the salt into the amide.
steps.margin_note: Write both equations. The Δ over the second arrow is what the examiner looks for.

steps.label: Aniline to p-bromoaniline
steps.why: The –NH₂ group activates the ring so strongly that bromine water alone puts bromine at all three of the 2, 4 and 6 positions in one step. Acetylation turns –NH₂ into –NHCOCH₃, whose lone pair is shared with the carbonyl group, so the ring is less activated and only the para position reacts. Hydrolysis then returns the –NH₂ group unchanged.
common_mistakes: Brominating aniline directly. Bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, not the para product.
Stopping at p-bromoacetanilide. The last hydrolysis step is needed to get back to the amine.
steps.memory_tip: Protect, brominate, remove the protection: acetic anhydride on, bromine in at para, then hydrolyse the acetyl group off.
steps.margin_note: Three arrows, three reagents. Naming acetanilide and p-bromoacetanilide shows the route is understood.

insider_note: Route (ii) is marked as one route, not three separate reactions, so all three arrows must be there. The reason for the first arrow is what most answers leave out: without acetylation, aniline and bromine water give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline instead of the para product.
